facts: On the unit circle, the point at angle $\theta$ is $P(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$.
$\cos\theta$ is positive when $P$ is right of the $y$-axis and negative when $P$ is left of it.
$\sin\theta$ is positive when $P$ is above the $x$-axis and negative when $P$ is below it.
Every point on the unit circle satisfies $x^2+y^2=1$, so $\cos\theta$ and $\sin\theta$ always lie between $-1$ and $1$.

foundation.solution_text:
$\cos\theta$ is the $x$-coordinate of $P$ and $\sin\theta$ is the $y$-coordinate of $P$.
$\cos\theta=0.6$
$\sin\theta=0.8$

$\cos\theta$ is the $x$-coordinate and $\sin\theta$ is the $y$-coordinate. $P$ is left of the $y$-axis, so $x$ is negative.
$\cos\theta=-0.6$
$\sin\theta=0.8$

$\cos\theta$ is the $x$-coordinate and $\sin\theta$ is the $y$-coordinate. $P$ is below the $x$-axis, so $y$ is negative.
$\cos\theta=0.6$
$\sin\theta=-0.8$

foundation.question_text: State the exact coordinates of $P(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ when $\theta=90^{\circ}$, and hence write $\cos90^{\circ}$ and $\sin90^{\circ}$.
foundation.solution_text:
At $\theta=90^{\circ}$, $P$ sits at the top of the unit circle, $P=(0,1)$.
$\cos90^{\circ}=0$
$\sin90^{\circ}=1$

foundation.question_text: State the exact coordinates of $P(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ when $\theta=180^{\circ}$, and hence write $\cos180^{\circ}$ and $\sin180^{\circ}$.
foundation.solution_text:
At $\theta=180^{\circ}$, $P$ sits at the left of the unit circle, $P=(-1,0)$.
$\cos180^{\circ}=-1$
$\sin180^{\circ}=0$

foundation.question_text: The point $P(0.28,0.96)$ lies on the unit circle at angle of inclination $\theta$. State $\cos\theta$ and $\sin\theta$.
foundation.solution_text:
$\cos\theta$ is the $x$-coordinate and $\sin\theta$ is the $y$-coordinate of $P$.
$\cos\theta=0.28$
$\sin\theta=0.96$

foundation.question_text: The point $P(-0.96,0.28)$ lies on the unit circle at angle of inclination $\theta$. State $\cos\theta$ and $\sin\theta$.
foundation.solution_text:
$\cos\theta$ is the $x$-coordinate and $\sin\theta$ is the $y$-coordinate of $P$.
$\cos\theta=-0.96$
$\sin\theta=0.28$

development.question_text: State the exact coordinates of $P(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ when $\theta=270^{\circ}$, and hence write $\cos270^{\circ}$ and $\sin270^{\circ}$.
development.solution_text:
At $\theta=270^{\circ}$, $P$ sits at the bottom of the unit circle, $P=(0,-1)$.
$\cos270^{\circ}=0$

development.question_text: The point $P(-0.6,-0.8)$ lies on the unit circle at angle of inclination $\theta$. State $\cos\theta$ and $\sin\theta$, and name the quadrant $P$ is in.
development.solution_text:
$\cos\theta$ is the $x$-coordinate and $\sin\theta$ is the $y$-coordinate of $P$.
$\cos\theta=-0.6$
$\sin\theta=-0.8$
Both coordinates are negative, so $P$ is in the third quadrant.

$\cos\theta$ is the $x$-coordinate of $P$.
In the second quadrant $P$ lies to the left of the $y$-axis, so its $x$-coordinate is negative.
Therefore $\cos\theta$ is negative.

development.question_text: A point on the unit circle has $\cos\theta=-1$ and $\sin\theta=0$. State the angle $\theta$ in $0^{\circ}\le\theta<360^{\circ}$ and the coordinates of $P$.
development.solution_text:

mastery.question_text: The point $P(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ lies on the unit circle with $\cos\theta=0.6$, and $\theta$ is in the first quadrant. Find $\sin\theta$.
mastery.solution_text:
Every point on the unit circle satisfies $x^2+y^2=1$, with $x=\cos\theta$ and $y=\sin\theta$.
$\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta$
$=1-0.6^2$
$=1-0.36$
$=0.64$
$\sin\theta=\pm0.8$
In the first quadrant $y>0$, so $\sin\theta=0.8$.

mastery.question_text: The point $P(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ lies on the unit circle with $\sin\theta=-0.28$, and $\theta$ is in the third quadrant. Find $\cos\theta$.
mastery.solution_text:
Every point on the unit circle satisfies $x^2+y^2=1$, with $x=\cos\theta$ and $y=\sin\theta$.
$\cos^2\theta=1-\sin^2\theta$
$=1-(-0.28)^2$
$=1-0.0784$
$=0.9216$
$\cos\theta=\pm0.96$
In the third quadrant $x<0$, so $\cos\theta=-0.96$.

mastery.question_text: A student claims a point on the unit circle has $\cos\theta=1.2$. Explain why this is impossible.
mastery.solution_text:
$\cos\theta$ is the $x$-coordinate of a point on a circle of radius $1$ centred at the origin.
Every point on that circle has $-1\le x\le1$, so its $x$-coordinate can never be greater than $1$.
Therefore $\cos\theta=1.2$ is impossible.
